questions.text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers?
questions.solution:
Checking each BST claim for [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers:

- Maximum path length from root to any node is [latex]n-1[/latex]: true — in the worst case (a completely skewed/degenerate BST, essentially a linked list), all [latex]n[/latex] nodes form a single chain, giving a root-to-deepest-node path of [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, which is also the largest this can ever be since there are only [latex]n[/latex] nodes total.
- Inorder traversal always produces sorted order: true — this is the defining property of a BST (left subtree [latex]<[/latex] node [latex]<[/latex] right subtree, recursively), and it holds regardless of the tree's shape.
- Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2n)[/latex] time in the worst case: false — that bound only holds for a balanced BST. A skewed/degenerate BST (as noted above) can force search time all the way up to [latex]O(n)[/latex].
- Every BST is also a Min-Heap: false — a min-heap requires every parent to be smaller than both children, but a BST only orders left [latex]<[/latex] parent [latex]<[/latex] right; nothing stops a BST's left child from being smaller than its grandparent in ways that violate heap order.

Answer: Max path length is n-1; and inorder traversal always gives sorted order.

Click here for detail solution
options: The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is [latex](n - 1)[/latex].
An inorder traversal will always produce a sorted sequence of elements.
Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2 n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
Every BST is also a Min-Heap.

questions.text: Consider the following [latex]B^+[/latex] tree with 5 nodes, in which a node can store at most 3 key values. The value 23 is now inserted in the [latex]B^+[/latex] tree. Which of the following options(s) is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Inserting a new key into a [latex]B^+[/latex] tree always follows the same pattern: search down to the correct leaf, insert the key there in sorted order, and if that leaf now holds more than the maximum allowed keys (here, more than [latex]3[/latex]), it must split into two leaves, pushing/copying up a separator key into the parent.

Since the target leaf here is already at its maximum capacity of [latex]3[/latex] keys before inserting [latex]23[/latex], it overflows and must split; this new separator key then gets inserted into the parent node, which can itself overflow and split further, potentially propagating all the way up to a new root. Whenever a split reaches (or creates a new) root, the height of the tree increases by one level. Splitting always increases the total node count (a leaf becomes two, or an internal node splits into two) — it never leaves the count unchanged, and "no node splits" is only possible if the target leaf had spare capacity, which it did not here.

Answer: At least one node will split and redistribute; and the height of the tree will increase.

Click here for detail solution
options: None of the nodes will split.
At least one node will split and redistribute.
The total number of nodes will remain same.
The height of the tree will increase.

questions.text:
Let S1 and S2 be two stacks. S1 has capacity of 4 elements. S2 has capacity of 2 elements. S1 already has 4 elements: 100, 200, 300, and 400, whereas S2 is empty, as shown below.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|} \hline 400 (Top) \\ \hline 300 \\ \hline 200\\ \hline 100 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
Stack S1

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|} \hline \\ \hline \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
Stack S2

Only the following three operations are available:

PushToS2: Pop the top element from S1 and push it on S2.
PushToS1: Pop the top element from S2 and push it on S1.
GenerateOutput: Pop the top element from S1 and output it to the user.

Note that the pop operation is not allowed on an empty stack and the push operation is not allowed on a full stack.

Which of the following output sequences can be generated by using the above operations?
questions.solution:
S1 = 100, 200, 300, 400 (top). S2 can hold only 2 elements.

- 100, 200, 400, 300: to output 100 first, 400, 300, 200 (3 elements) must go to S2 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] impossible.
- 200, 300, 400, 100: move 400, 300 to S2; output 200; move 300 back, output 300; move 400 back, output 400; output 100 True
- 400, 200, 100, 300: output 400; move 300 to S2; output 200, 100; move 300 back, output 300 True
- 300, 200, 400, 100: move 400 to S2; output 300, 200; move 400 back, output 400; output 100 True

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.text:
You are given a set [latex]V[/latex] of distinct integers. A binary search tree [latex]T[/latex] is created by inserting all elements of [latex]V[/latex] one by one, starting with an empty tree. The tree [latex]T[/latex] follows the convention that, at each node, all values stored in the left subtree of the node are smaller than the value stored at the node. You are not aware of the sequence in which these values were inserted into [latex]T[/latex], and you do not have access to [latex]T[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
The inorder traversal of any BST is the keys in sorted order, whatever the insertion order. So it can be found from V just by sorting.

Root, preorder and postorder depend on the insertion order. Example V = {1, 2}: inserting 1 then 2 gives root 1; inserting 2 then 1 gives root 2.

Answer: Inorder traversal of T can be determined from V

questions.text: Let [latex] A [/latex] be an array containing integer values. The distance of [latex] A [/latex] is defined as the minimum number of elements in [latex] A [/latex] that must be replaced with another integer so that the resulting array is sorted in non-decreasing order. The distance of the array [latex] [2,5,3,1,4,2,6] [/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
Elements we keep must already be in non-decreasing order; all others can be replaced by suitable values. So
distance = [latex]n-[/latex] (length of longest non-decreasing subsequence).

In [2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 6] the longest non-decreasing subsequence is 2, 3, 4, 6 (length 4).

Distance [latex]=7-4=3[/latex] (e.g. [2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 6]).

Answer: 3
